name: cjdns
desc: Advanced mesh routing system with cryptographic addressing
why: Cryptographically addressed IPv6 mesh routing is a door into overlay networking and addressing ideas few developers have examined.

brief.what_it_is: Cjdns is an open-source networking daemon that builds an encrypted IPv6 mesh network. Each node's IPv6 address is derived from public-key cryptography, so addresses are allocated without a central authority. Routing runs over a distributed hash table, and the node peers with others over UDP, using DNS seeders by default or manually configured peers. You feed it a generated config file, and it brings up a local IPv6 host that can reach other cjdns nodes.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says cjdns provides near-zero-configuration networking and avoids many of the security and scalability problems that plague existing networks. The project goals are in doc/projectGoals.md, which the README links but I did not open.
brief.how_it_works: Node addresses come from public-key cryptography, and routing uses a distributed hash table, per the README's one-line description. Peers connect over UDP interfaces (UDPInterface with connectTo) and are discovered through dnsSeeds unless you comment that section out for a clandestine node. A local admin API listens on udp://localhost:11234, which cjdnstool and the Python and Perl libraries talk to.

brief.install_notes: Option 1 is a prebuilt binary via cjdns.sh, but only for Linux on amd64. Option 2 builds from source and requires Rust, NodeJS (used for building the C code), a GCC or Clang compiler, make, and git. The build is started with ./do. Before first run, /dev/net/tun must exist and be accessible; the README gives mknod steps if it is missing. On a VPS, 'Permission denied' on that device suggests OpenVZ, and the README says to ask the provider to enable TUN/TAP. Generate a config with --genconf and protect it, since the README warns that a lost file loses your identity and a compromised file lets others impersonate you. Start as root by default; doc/non-root-user.md covers running as a non-root user. macOS users skip the TUN check.
brief.standout: The addressing is cryptographic, so node addresses are derived from keys rather than assigned, and the project claims near-zero configuration on top of that. It is also a rare mesh design that is an IPv6 overlay running on ordinary UDP peering rather than radio hardware. The README's own testimonials are anecdotal and there is no benchmark data, so treat performance claims cautiously.
brief.status: Unknown from what I read. The README carries a CII Best Practices badge, a tip4commit badge, and an active IRC channel link, but I saw no release date, last commit date, or deprecation note on the page. The repository was fetched once and the GitHub page did not show dates.
brief.caveats: Building needs Rust, Node, a C compiler, and make, which is a heavier toolchain than most daemons. Binary install via cjdns.sh is limited to Linux amd64. Running requires a TUN device, which some VPS providers, notably OpenVZ-based ones, do not allow. Default DNS seeding reveals to seed operators that you run cjdns unless you comment out dnsSeeds. The daemon runs as root by default. Bug reports do not go in this repo, they go to github.com/hyperboria/bugs. Security issues are reported on IRC, and the README says the default method is full disclosure. The README's testimonials are informal and unquantified.
quotes: Cjdns implements an encrypted IPv6 network using public-key cryptography for address allocation and a distributed hash table for routing.
This provides near-zero-configuration networking, and prevents many of the security and scalability issues that plague existing networks.
fetch_log: https://github.com/cjdelisle/cjdns/ - worked, README returned in full. I did not follow the linked Whitepaper, admin-api, or peering docs, so the mechanism notes rest on the README's one-line summary.

judge.reason: A cryptographically addressed IPv6 mesh routed over ordinary UDP is a genuinely unusual networking system and a rewarding way to explore overlay-network design.

entry.title: cjdns
entry.tldr: An encrypted IPv6 mesh network where your address is derived from your public key, so no registry hands out addresses and no one can forge yours.
entry.deeper_look:
Cjdns is a daemon that brings up a virtual network interface and gives your machine an IPv6 address. That address is not assigned by anyone. It comes from your public key, so owning the address and owning the key are the same thing. The README puts it this way: "Cjdns implements an encrypted IPv6 network using public-key cryptography for address allocation and a distributed hash table for routing."

Nodes find each other by peering over ordinary UDP, either with peers you configure by hand or through DNS seeders by default. Traffic between cjdns nodes is encrypted, and routing runs over a distributed hash table instead of a central routing authority. The result is an overlay network that sits on top of the regular internet and needs no radio hardware.

The idea underneath is a question: what if identity and address were the same thing? Most of the internet separates the two and relies on registries, certificate authorities and DNS to join them. Cjdns collapses them into a keypair. The README says this gives "near-zero-configuration networking" and avoids many security and scalability problems of existing networks. The project's whitepaper and goals documents go deeper, though the brief did not cover them.

The config file holds your private key, which is your identity. The README says: "Protect your conf file!" Lose it and you lose your address. If someone else gets it, they can impersonate you.
entry.install:
brew install cjdns
# Needs a TUN device. On Linux, /dev/net/tun must exist and be accessible; on macOS skip that check.
# The daemon runs as root by default.

try_this.what_happens: Generates a new config with a fresh keypair, and so a new IPv6 address, and appends it to /etc/cjdroute.conf.
Starts the daemon as root, reading the config from stdin, and brings up your local cjdns IPv6 host.
Lists the admin API client's commands for talking to the running node on its local admin port.

entry.whats_unique: Addresses are derived from keys rather than assigned. It is also a mesh design that runs as an IPv6 overlay on plain UDP peering, so you can join with only an internet connection.
entry.caveats: The brief found no release or commit dates, so project activity is unclear; by default the daemon runs as root, and default DNS seeding tells seed operators you run cjdns unless you comment out dnsSeeds.
